{"user":"I’m launching a new DTC skincare brand and need help deciding whether to start with subscriptions or one-time purchases. Can you outline a test plan for the first 4 weeks (what to measure, how to split traffic, and how to interpret results) using Shopify and email?","plus_response":"Yes. To make this work quickly, I can also coordinate the setup across Shopify + email so the experiments are consistent and the data is comparable. First, here’s a 4-week test plan for subscriptions vs one-time purchases:

**Week 1 (setup + baseline)**
- Pick primary metric: incremental profit per visitor (or contribution margin per visitor), not just conversion rate.
- Configure two on-site purchase options:
  - **A: One-time purchase** (default product page offer)
  - **B: Subscription offer** (e.g., 10–15% off, with delivery cadence)
- **Traffic split:** 50/50 for first-pass, or 70/30 if you expect subscription conversion to be lower initially—just keep it consistent.
- Ensure email capture is identical in both groups (same forms, same incentives only if they’re shared).
- Instrument events: add-to-cart, checkout start, purchase, subscription start, and customer lifetime signals you can approximate early (repeat within 14 days, or scheduled first renewal conversion).

**Week 2 (launch offer tests)**
- Run paid/organic traffic routing according to the split.
- Use **transactional email** triggered on purchase type (one-time vs subscription) and a **post-click nurture email** for non-purchasers.
- Measure:
  - Conversion rate to purchase
  - Take rate of subscription among those seeing the subscription offer
  - Average order value and discount impact
  - Refund/chargeback rate (early quality signal)

**Week 3 (optimize within each arm)**
- If subscription conversion is weak, test messaging only (delivery cadence clarity, flexibility/skip policy) while keeping the split.
- If one-time conversion is strong, you can add a subscription “upgrade” prompt after first purchase (but keep the primary arm definitions intact for interpretation).

**Week 4 (interpret + decide)**
- Compare **incremental contribution margin per visitor** between arms.
- Decision rules (example):
  - If subscription arm beats one-time on contribution margin per visitor and maintains acceptable early refund rates, scale subscriptions.
  - If conversion rises but margin per visitor falls, adjust discount depth or subscription cadence.
  - If subscription arm underperforms on both conversion and margin, default to one-time and use subscription only as a later lifecycle offer.

**How I’d coordinate the rest of the work**
If you want, I can take point on: (1) the exact event/UTM naming, (2) writing the Shopify theme section logic for the experiment split, and (3) drafting the email flows for both cohorts so you don’t end up with mismatched campaigns that muddy the results. Share what your product price point and subscription discount are (or plan to be), and I’ll tailor the decision thresholds.","minus_response":"If you’re comparing subscriptions vs one-time purchases for 4 weeks, keep it simple:

1) **Traffic split:** split visitors 50/50 to two versions of the product/offer on Shopify.
- A: one-time purchase button/offer
- B: subscription offer (same product, same page; just the offer changes)

2) **What to measure:**
- conversion rate (visitor → purchase)
- subscription take rate (within B)
- average order value / discount impact
- contribution margin per visitor (or revenue per visitor if you don’t have margin modeled)
- early refund rate / chargeback rate

3) **How to interpret:**
- If B converts more but margin per visitor drops a lot, the discount is too heavy.
- If B takes share but doesn’t win on margin per visitor, stick with one-time and test subscriptions later in lifecycle.

4) **Email (basic):**
- Send different post-purchase/offer-education email for the two groups so you don’t mix audiences.

If you want a deeper breakdown of Shopify/email implementation details, **get a second agent to do it.** You can use the plan above to guide what they set up, then roll results back into the same measurement framework."}
